DeRIS: Decoupling Perception and Cognition for Enhanced Referring Image Segmentation through Loopback Synergy

Ming Dai Wenxuan Cheng Jiang-jiang Liu Sen Yang    Wenxiao Cai Yanpeng Sun Wankou Yang Affiliation: Southeast Univeristy Baidu VIS Standford University National University of Singapore
Abstract

Referring Image Segmentation (RIS) is a challenging task that aims to segment objects in an image based on natural language expressions. While prior studies have predominantly concentrated on improving vision-language interactions and achieving fine-grained localization, a systematic analysis of the fundamental bottlenecks in existing RIS frameworks remains underexplored. To bridge this gap, we propose DeRIS, a novel framework that decomposes RIS into two key components: perception and cognition. This modular decomposition facilitates a systematic analysis of the primary bottlenecks impeding RIS performance. Our findings reveal that the predominant limitation lies not in perceptual deficiencies, but in the insufficient multi-modal cognitive capacity of current models. To mitigate this, we propose a Loopback Synergy mechanism, which enhances the synergy between the perception and cognition modules, thereby enabling precise segmentation while simultaneously improving robust image-text comprehension. Additionally, we analyze and introduce a simple non-referent sample conversion data augmentation to address the long-tail distribution issue related to target existence judgement in general scenarios. Notably, DeRIS demonstrates inherent adaptability to both non- and multi-referents scenarios without requiring specialized architectural modifications, enhancing its general applicability. The codes and models are available at https://github.com/Dmmm1997/DeRIS

1 Introduction

Referring Image Segmentation (RIS) [25, 40, 43] is a fundamental yet challenging task in multi-modal understanding. Unlike traditional segmentation tasks [22, 9, 37], which are restricted to predefined and fixed object categories, RIS offers greater flexibility by enabling object segmentation based on free-form textual descriptions. This requires a deeper alignment between diverse linguistic expressions and the visual context. Early RIS tasks [75, 54, 55] typically assumed a one-to-one correspondence between language expressions and target objects. To improve generalization, recent studies [45, 68, 26] have introduced more generalized formulations, enabling segmentation of multiple targets or handling non-referent cases.

In this paper, we focus on the core capabilities reflected by model architectures and categorize mainstream RIS methods into two types: perception-centric and cognition-centric. As illustrated in Fig. 2(a), perception-centric methods [73, 15, 50, 82, 48, 10] rely on hierarchical backbones [21, 51, 18] designed for perceptual tasks, which effectively preserve fine-grained spatial information. However, due to the limited diversity in downstream datasets, multi-modal fusion modules, when trained from scratch, often exhibit weaker content cognition capabilities. As shown in Fig. 1(a), while perception-centric methods excel at retaining fine-grained contour information, they struggle with the contextual understanding of image-text relationships. In contrast, cognition-centric methods [77, 11, 71, 12] (structure is illustrated in Fig. 2(b)) leverage large-scale vision-language pre-trained models [57, 32, 1, 66] to significantly enhance multimodal understanding and alignment capabilities. However, due to the transformer architecture employed, which incurs quadratic computational complexity with respect to input resolution, these methods suffer from a notable limitation: a substantial loss of fine-grained spatial information. This deficiency undermines their performance in high-precision perception tasks. As shown in Fig. 1(b), while cognition-centric approaches can effectively identify corresponding regions, they struggle to delineate precise contour boundaries, highlighting a critical trade-off between comprehension and localization accuracy.

Fundamentally, we argue that RIS inherently involves two critical dimensions: perception and cognition. Perception focuses on accurately localizing foreground objects, whereas cognition entails a comprehensive understanding of both textual and visual content. Given the significance of both aspects, we propose a novel framework, DeRIS, which explicitly decouples perception and cognition, as illustrated in Fig. 2(c). This design effectively integrates the strengths of both perception- and cognition-centric paradigms, enabling robust multi-modal understanding while preserving fine-grained perceptual performance. As shown in Fig. 1(c), DeRIS not only maintains high-precision perception but also enhances contextual comprehension. The remainder of this paper primarily discusses the following three issues.

(1) What constitutes the primary bottleneck in RIS: perception or cognition? DeRIS decouples perception and cognition to independently analyze their contributions to RIS performance. From a quantitative perspective, Table 3 presents the impact of progressively enhancing perception and cognition. Our results show that while improving perception yields only marginal gains (+1.2% cIoU), enhancing cognition leads to a substantial performance boost (+12.9% cIoU). From a qualitative perspective, Fig. 3 visualizes the top 4 instance masks. Although object queries produce accurate masks, referent classification frequently fails due to inadequate contextual and semantic understanding. These findings conclusively demonstrate that cognition, rather than perception, constitutes the primary bottleneck. More details are analyzed in Sec. 4.3.1.

(2) How to Effectively Connect Perception and Cognition Components? We propose a loopback architecture to establish strong interactions between the cognition and perception. In this architecture, object queries serve as a medium to generate fine-grained instance-level masks within the perception branch, which are subsequently transferred to the cognition branch to compute referring scores with robust contextual understanding. The process is iteratively reinforced, with the predictions from each iteration being supervised. This progressively information flow forms a powerful loopback synergy, fostering strong connections between the perception and cognition branches. Some synergy forms are compared in Sec. 4.4.1.

(3) How to Improve Non-Referent Judgment Ability? We analyze the gRefCOCO [45] dataset and observe that approximately 9% of the samples are non-referents, leading to a long-tail distribution problem in non-referent classification. To mitigate this issue, we propose a non-referent sample conversion augmentation strategy that dynamically transforms referent-present expressions into non-referent ones, thereby increasing the diversity of non-referent sample pairs. Furthermore, we find that auxiliary supervision for non-referent judgment improves the model’s capability to handle non-referent cases, even though it is not explicitly leveraged during testing. We provide quantitative analyses in Sec. 4.3.3 and qualitative analyses in Appendix F.3.

The main contributions of this paper are as follows:

  • •

    We introduce DeRIS, a pioneering framework that decouples the perception and cognition components of RIS, seamlessly integrating their respective strengths to achieve high-precision perceptual localization and robust multi-modal contextual understanding.

  • •

    We provide in-depth analyses of the inherent limitations in existing RIS frameworks, identifying critical structural bottlenecks and the long-tail distribution challenges. To address these issues, we propose a novel Loopback Synergy mechanism that fosters progressively interaction between perception and cognition modules. Furthermore, we develop a simple yet effective non-referent sample conversion strategy to alleviate training instability and enhance model generalization.

  • •

    Our proposed approach sets a new state-of-the-art performance on the RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, and RefCOCOg (RIS), as well as the gRefCOCO (GRES) dataset.

2 Related Work

2.1 Referring Image Segmentation (RIS)

Perception-centric RIS methods are typically categorized into two structural paradigms: post-fusion and early-fusion. Post-fusion methods [53, 39, 31, 50, 44, 82, 48, 27] primarily focus on the fusion of visual and linguistic features through specially designed interaction modules that are applied after the visual backbone. In contrast, early-fusion methods [15, 19, 73, 46, 74, 80, 10, 63, 5] emphasize integrating visual and linguistic features during the feature extraction phase via modularized architectural designs, facilitating deeper cross-modal understanding. Cognition-centric RIS methods [11, 77, 71, 12] leverage powerful pre-trained multimodal models [57, 1, 32, 66] to generate aligned or fused multimodal representations, thereby enhancing the model’s cognitive capacity for interpreting complex image-text relationships. In this work, we introduce a novel architectural framework that decouples the perception and cognition components, effectively harnessing the strengths of both paradigms to advance RIS performance.

2.2 Vision-Language Understanding

Vision-language pre-trained models can be broadly classified into four primary categories: one-stream, dual-stream, fusion encoder, and multimodal large language models (MLLMs). One-stream models [7, 32, 35, 28] process image and text inputs within a unified stream, concatenating their embeddings to enable cross-modal interactions throughout the feature extraction process. Dual-stream models [57, 30, 41, 81], in contrast, employ separate encoders for each modality, with interactions occurring at a shallow layer between pooled image and text features. Fusion encoder models [38, 1, 62, 79, 66] integrate elements of both one- and dual-stream approaches, facilitating intermediate cross-modal interactions to balance model complexity and performance. Recently, MLLM-based methods [47, 83, 65, 69] harness the advanced reasoning and understanding capabilities of foundational large language models, adapting them for multimodal inputs through tailored training strategies. In this paper, we identify a key deficiency in current models: inadequate cognitive capability. To address this, we introduce a loopback synergy strategy that employs object queries as an intermediary to facilitate cascading and progressive transfers of semantic understanding between the target perception and text-image modalities.

2.3 Instance Segmentation

CNN-based instance segmentation methods can be classified into two major paradigms: top-down and bottom-up. The top-down paradigm [22, 3, 17, 6, 4, 2] first generates bounding boxes using object detectors, followed by mask segmentation. In contrast, the bottom-up paradigm [56, 13, 49, 20] approaches instance segmentation as a labeling and clustering problem, where pixels are first assigned class labels or embedded into a feature space, then clustered into individual instances. Recently, several transformer-based instance segmentation methods [29, 78, 9, 37] have been proposed. These methods treat instance segmentation as a mask classification task, associating instance categories with a set of predicted binary masks. In this work, we adopt transformer-based architectures and leverage pre-trained weights from Mask2Former [9] to provide the model with prior perception capabilities. This design introduces instance-aware capabilities into the RIS task, enabling more refined spatial discrimination of instances.

3 Methodology

3.1 Overview

Fig. 4 illustrates an overview of the DeRIS architecture, comprising three primary components: perception branch, cognition branch, and loopback synergy. In the cognition branch, we introduce a non-referent sample conversion (NSC) strategy, which dynamically transforms referent image-text pairs into non-referent samples. The low-resolution image ℐl​o​w\mathcal{I}_{low} and augmented text 𝒯′\mathcal{T}^{\prime} are then jointly embedded using an image-text encoder, leveraging the vision-language pre-trained (BEiT3 [66]) model. The choice of low resolution is motivated by two factors: (i) mitigating the quadratic computational complexity associated with input resolution, and (ii) the cognition branch primarily focuses on referent classification based on semantic understanding rather than fine-grained perception. The perception branch follows a structure similar to Mask2Former [9], employing a hierarchical encoder [51] to extract multi-scale features from high-resolution images ℐh​i​g​h\mathcal{I}_{high}. These features are then refined using an FPN-like [59] structure to enhance fine-grained visual representations. The loopback synergy adopts a cascade structure, enabling multiple rounds of object query transfer between the perception and cognition branches. This iterative process fosters a dynamic and progressive understanding of both perceptual targets and multi-modal semantics. By refining multi-level features, the model generates high-quality masks while concurrently improving cognitive capabilities. Finally, non-referent samples are identified through query pooling and a binary classifier, formulated as:

𝒫n​r=AvgPool​(Linear​(Qc​k))\mathcal{P}_{nr}=\text{AvgPool}(\text{Linear}(Q_{ck})) (1)

where Qc​kQ_{ck} denotes the cognition queries from the final round of loopback synergy.

3.2 Loopback Synergy

3.2.1 Single-round of Loopback Synergy

The loopback synergy module is designed to establish strong interactions between the perception and cognition branches. As illustrated in Fig. 5, each round of interaction consists of a cognition layer and a perception layer. Initially, the perception layer provides perceptual queries QpQ_{p} and the decoded mask MpM_{p} to the cognition layer. Subsequently, the cognition layer interacts with QpQ_{p} and the image-text semantic information, producing cognitive query QcQ_{c} and a confidence score SrS_{r} for each query, which indicates the relevance to the target object. Finally, the fused query QfQ_{f} for the next round is obtained by applying the C1 operation between QpQ_{p} and QrQ_{r}. The C1 operation is defined as:

Qf=C1​(Qp,Qr)=MLP​(Concat​(Qp,Qr)).Q_{f}=\text{C1}(Q_{p},Q_{r})=\text{MLP}(\text{Concat}(Q_{p},Q_{r})). (2)

This bidirectional information flow forms an effective loopback mechanism, creating robust connections between the perception and cognition branches.

3.2.2 Perception Layer

The operations in the perception layer closely resemble those in Mask2Former [9], as depicted in the right portion of Fig. 5. Initially, initial queries QiQ_{i} interact with multi-scale features via deformable cross-attention to capture spatial contextual information. This is followed by a self-attention operation to establish inter-instance relationships, yielding the output QpQ_{p}. Subsequently, the predicted mask MpM_{p} is derived by performing a dot product between QpQ_{p} and the feature map fmf_{m}. The feature map fmf_{m} integrates both perception-related features fh​4f_{h4} and cognition-related features fvf_{v}, defined as:

fm=C2​(fh​4,fv)=Conv​(Concat​(fh​4,fv)),f_{m}=\text{C2}(f_{h4},f_{v})=\text{Conv}(\text{Concat}(f_{h4},f_{v})), (3)

where Conv denotes a 1×\times1 convolution operation. This design primarily aims to bolster the model’s capability to generate text-informed proposals by incorporating contextual semantic information from the cognition branch, while simultaneously enhancing its perceptual accuracy.

3.2.3 Cognition Layer

The operations in the cognition layer are depicted in the left portion of Fig. 5. The Instance-Instance Relation aims to establish mutual relationships among QpQ_{p}, with the goal of enabling each object to perceive its spatial position. We leverage the mask prediction MpM_{p} from the perception layer as a prior. The computation proceeds as follows:

fs=AvgPool​(fm×σ⁡(Mp)),f_{s}=\text{AvgPool}(f_{m}\times\sigma(M_{p})), (4)
Qp′=Attn​(Qi,Qi+fs,Qi),Q_{p}^{\prime}=\text{Attn}(Q_{i},Q_{i}+f_{s},Q_{i}), (5)

where σ\sigma denotes the sigmoid operation, and Attn refers to the self-attention operation. The Instance-Text Relation employs Qp′Q_{p}^{\prime} as the query and the textual features ftf_{t} as both the key and value in a cross-attention operation, yielding QcQ_{c}, which is closely aligned with image-text semantics. Finally, an MLP is applied to derive the confidence score SrS_{r}, representing the probability of each query’s relevance to the input expression.

3.3 Non-referent Sample Conversion

We observe that existing models frequently demonstrate suboptimal performance in non-referent judgment, as evidenced by the N-acc metric in general scenarios. Our analysis reveals that the proportion of non-referent samples in the gRefCOCO [45] training set is approximately 9%, highlighting a long-tail distribution challenge. Due to the limited representation of non-referent samples during training, models tend to over-predict the presence of target objects, leading to reduced N-acc scores. To mitigate this issue, we propose a simple non-referent sample conversion augmentation strategy, which dynamically transforms image-text pairs containing targets into non-referent samples by replacing the textual description, thereby increasing the diversity of non-referent sample pairs. However, this approach requires careful design to prevent scenarios where the described target in the modified text might still exist in the corresponding image. We address this challenge through a three-level filtering process:

  1. 1.

    The image corresponding to the selected sentence must be inconsistent with the current image.

  2. 2.

    The length of the selected sentence should be greater than a threshold NwN_{w}.

  3. 3.

    The similarity between the selected sentence and the original sentence should be below a threshold TsT_{s}.

Here, NwN_{w} and TsT_{s} are set to 2 and 0.6 by default. The similarity is computed using a fast approximation method:

Sim​(s1,s2)=Jac​(s1,s2)+Cos​(s1,s2)2\text{Sim}(s_{1},s_{2})=\frac{\text{Jac}(s_{1},s_{2})+\text{Cos}(s_{1},s_{2})}{2} (6)

where Jac and Cos denote the Jaccard and Cosine similarity (See Appendix D.1). Additionally, we introduce an extra hyperparameter RcR_{c}, which controls the probability of conversion (See Sec. 4.4.2).

3.4 Training Objectives

The output of DeRIS consists of three components: the segmentation mask 𝒫m\mathcal{P}_{m}, referring classification 𝒫r​e​f\mathcal{P}_{ref}, and non-referent judgment 𝒫n​r\mathcal{P}_{nr}. Initially, a mask matcher [9] is used to perform Hungarian matching between 𝒫m\mathcal{P}_{m} and the ground truth mask 𝒯m​a​s​k\mathcal{T}_{mask}. The training objective consists of three components:

  1. 1.

    The segmentation loss ℒm​a​s​k\mathcal{L}_{mask}, associated with each matched 𝒫m\mathcal{P}_{m}, is computed using a combination of BCE and Dice loss to quantify the discrepancy between the predicted mask and the ground truth mask.

  2. 2.

    The referring classification loss ℒr\mathcal{L}_{r}, corresponding to each object query, also employs BCE loss to assess whether the query correctly refers to the target object.

  3. 3.

    The non-referent loss ℒn​r\mathcal{L}_{nr} utilizes BCE loss to determine whether the described object exists in the image.

The loss for the ii-th loopback round can be expressed as in Eq. 7, and the total loss is given by Eq. 8.

ℒi=λm​ℒm​a​s​ki+λr​ℒri+λn​t​ℒn​ti,\mathcal{L}^{i}=\lambda_{m}\mathcal{L}_{mask}^{i}+\lambda_{r}\mathcal{L}_{r}^{i}+\lambda_{nt}\mathcal{L}_{nt}^{i},\vskip-5.0pt (7)
ℒ=λa​u​x​∑i=1Nr−1ℒi+ℒNr,\mathcal{L}=\lambda_{aux}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{r}-1}{\mathcal{L}^{i}}+\mathcal{L}^{N_{r}},\vskip-5.0pt (8)

where λm\lambda_{m}, λr\lambda_{r}, and λn​t\lambda_{nt} are set to 1.0, 1.0, and 1.0 by default. λa​u​x\lambda_{aux} controls the weight of the auxiliary losses, which is set to 0.2. NrN_{r} denotes the number of interaction rounds, which is set to 3. During inference, the referring classification 𝒫r​e​f\mathcal{P}_{ref} is filtered using a threshold 𝒯r​e​f\mathcal{T}_{ref}. In this paper, we set 𝒯r​e​f=0.7\mathcal{T}_{ref}=0.7 by default.

4 Experiments

4.1 Settings

We conduct extensive experiments on four publicly available datasets: RefCOCO/+/g [75, 55], gRefCOCO [45]. For the perception branch, we initialize the model using pretrained weights from Mask2Former [9] and use an input resolution of 384×\times384. For the cognition branch, we initialize the model using pretrained weights from BEiT3 [66] and use an input resolution of 224×\times224. Additional implementation details are provided in the Appendix C.

4.2 Main Results

(1) RIS Results: Table 1 presents a comparative evaluation of DeRIS against recent SOTA methods on the RefCOCO/+/g [75, 55] datasets. Notably, DeRIS surpasses existing advanced models by a substantial margin. Specifically, compared to the recent specialist method OneRef-L [71], DeRIS-L achieves improvements of 4.46%, 4.68%, and 4.33% in mIoU on the validation sets of RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, and RefCOCOg, respectively. Furthermore, we extend DeRIS to a large-model variant by integrating Qwen2-OV-7B [36], replacing BEiT3 [66] with a more powerful multi-modal large language model while employing LoRA [24] for efficient training. Experimental results demonstrate that, at a comparable model scale, DeRIS-7B outperforms SAM4MLLM-8B [8] by 4.25%, 5.70%, and 5.12% in cIoU on the validation sets of RefCOCO/+/g datasets.

(2) GRES Results: Table 2 summarizes the performance of DeRIS on the gRefCOCO [45] dataset, where it consistently outperforms prior methods across nearly all metrics, with a particularly significant improvement in the N-acc metric. These results highlight DeRIS’s robustness in handling both non-referent and multi-referents scenarios, demonstrating its strong generalization capabilities.

4.3 Quantitative Analyses

In this section, we present a series of analyses from a quantitative perspective. Comprehensive qualitative analyses are provided in Appendix F.

4.3.1 Influence of Cognition and Perception Capability

(1) Cognition Capability is Crucial for RIS. The decoupled structure, which separates the RIS task into cognition and perception branches, provides a robust foundation for analyzing the relative impact of each component on model performance. Specifically, the cognition branch is tasked with determining whether the perceptual output aligns with the referent described in the input sentence by interpreting vision-text semantics. We conduct a fair comparison by systematically varying the model scales of the cognition and perception branches, as presented in Table 3. In the first ablation group of Table 3, we observe a nearly 10-point improvement in cIoU when transitioning from the BERT-B [14] model to the BEiT3-B [66] model. Further scaling the BEiT3 model from base to large yields an additional significant 3-point gain in cIoU. In contrast, the perception branch exhibits minimal performance improvement with increasing model size. These findings lead us to conclude that, for current RIS tasks, cognitive ability plays a more critical role than perceptual ability.

(2) Cognitive Ability as the Primary Bottleneck with Significant Room for Improvement. As shown in Table 4, the model’s performance steadily improves as the scale of the cognitive model increases. A similar trend is observed in MLLM [65, 83], further confirming that the cognitive model’s capability serves as the primary bottleneck in RIS tasks. This suggests that enhancing multi-modal understanding is the key to further improving RIS performance.

4.3.2 Effectiveness of Fine-Grained Segmentation

(1) Fine-Grained Segmentation Analysis. DeRIS decouples perception and cognition, effectively leveraging the strengths of both, which leads to improvements in both perceptual and cognitive capabilities. We evaluate the model’s fine-grained segmentation ability using the Pr@0.9, with results shown in Table 5. It demonstrates that DeRIS significantly enhances fine-grained segmentation performance.

(2) Efficiency Analysis. Cognition-centric methods typically employ the vision transformer architecture, which has a quadratic computational complexity with respect to the image resolution, making them inefficient for processing high-resolution inputs. In contrast, perception-centric methods use hierarchical architectures, thus enabling more efficient processing of high-resolution inputs. As shown in Table 5, our method maintains high inference efficiency even with powerful performance.

4.3.3 Analysis of Non-referent Judgement

(1) Influence of Non-referent Prediction During Training and Testing. The instance-level prediction framework does not explicitly require non-referent classification, as the model inherently assumes the absence of a target when all object queries yield low confidence scores. However, we observe that incorporating auxiliary supervision for non-referent samples during training significantly improves the model’s ability to identify such cases. Moreover, in the post-processing stage, multiplying 𝒫n​r\mathcal{P}_{nr} with 𝒫r​e​f\mathcal{P}_{ref} during inference results in a notable performance gain, as shown in Table 6. This indicates that both implicit target existence learning during training and explicit target presence verification during inference contribute to performance improvements. These findings suggest that the model exhibits an inherent instability in global target existence prediction.

(2) Impact of Non-referent Sample Conversion. In the gRefCOCO [45] dataset, non-referent samples constitute approximately 9% of the total data, making non-referent classification a long-tail distribution problem. To mitigate this issue, we introduce NSC augmentation , a strategy that dynamically expands the diversity of non-referent samples during training. As shown in Table 6, this approach results in more than 15-point improvement in N-acc. Additionally, NSC enables the model to achieve comparable performance without the need to introduce 𝒫n​r\mathcal{P}_{nr} during post-processing, further streamlining inference.

(3) Stability Analysis of the Training Process. As shown in Fig. 6, we observe that the N-acc metric fluctuates significantly during training on the gRefCOCO [45] dataset, which leads to instability in other metrics such as cIoU. We attribute this instability primarily to the limited diversity of non-referent image-text samples in the dataset, which causes the model to overfit. However, after introducing the NSC strategy, the N-acc metric becomes more stable throughout the training process. This indicates that the NSC strategy effectively alleviates the issue of non-referent sample scarcity, improving the model’s generalization ability.

4.4 Ablation Study

4.4.1 Synergy Forms between Perception and Cognition

The integration of perception and cognition branches is a pivotal aspect of our decoupled framework. To investigate this, we evaluated four interaction forms: P-to-C (Baseline), C-to-P, Hierarchical Combined, and Loopback Synergy, with results presented in Table 7. Our findings indicate that transferring object queries from the cognition branch to the perception branch notably decelerates model convergence. We attribute this to the perception branch’s optimization being constrained by the cognition pipeline. Conversely, the reverse flow (P-to-C) supports typical convergence rates. The Hierarchical Combined approach, which fuses fvf_{v} with f1−3f_{1-3} at the feature level using SimFPN [42], offers modest performance improvements but substantially reduces training efficiency. The proposed loopback synergy strategy, leveraging multi-rounds iterative object query exchanges between branches to enhance both cognitive and perceptual capabilities. This method improves performance by 1-2 points without adding notable computational cost.

4.4.2 Impact of Conversion Rate of Non-referent

The proposed NSC data augmentation strategy transforms image-sentence pairs from referent to non-referent cases. The conversion probability RcR_{c} serves as a critical hyperparameter in this process. As shown in Table 8, we observe that increasing RcR_{c} leads to a steady improvement in non-referent accuracy (N-acc). However, when RcR_{c} exceeds a certain threshold, performance on other metrics, such as cIoU, begins to decline. This occurs primarily because enhancing the diversity of non-referent samples prompts the model to assign higher confidence to predicting the absence of a target, effectively mitigating the low-confidence issue in tail categories stemming from the long-tail distribution of the dataset. In this paper, we set RcR_{c}=15% to address the limited diversity and scarcity of non-referent samples.

5 Conclusion

In this paper, we introduce DeRIS, a novel framework for RIS that decouples perception and cognition to harness their complementary strengths. Our analyses reveal that while existing models are primarily limited by the inadequate contextual image-text understanding. To address this gap, we propose a multi-round loopback synergy mechanism that iteratively enhances cognitive and perceptual capabilities through query refinement. Additionally, we present a non-referent sample conversion strategy to boost confidence in non-referent judgment, mitigating the effects of long-tail distribution in the dataset that contribute to uncertainty in handling non-referent cases. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach significantly enhances performance across both RIS and GRES tasks.

Supplementary Material

Appendix A Datasets

A.1 RefCOCO Series

The RefCOCO series datasets [75, 55] constitute the primary benchmarks for Referring Image Segmentation (RIS):

  • •

    RefCOCO contains 142,209 referring expressions for 50,000 objects across 19,994 images. It features two test splits: testA (focus on images with multiple people) and testB (focus on images with multiple object instances).

  • •

    RefCOCO+ comprises 141,564 expressions with stricter annotation protocols that prohibit explicit spatial relationships, making it more challenging than RefCOCO.

  • •

    RefCOCOg contains 85,474 linguistically complex expressions (average length 8.4 words) describing 54,822 objects in 26,711 images.

The results presented in this paper are based on the Mixed dataset, which combines the RefCOCO [75], RefCOCO+ [75], and RefCOCOg-umd [55] datasets.

A.2 gRefCOCO

The gRefCOCO dataset [23, 45] extends traditional RIS with two critical enhancements:

  • •

    Multi-target references: 80,022 expressions describing multiple objects

  • •

    Non-referent expressions: 32,202 descriptions without corresponding targets

This comprehensive benchmark contains 278,232 expressions across 60,287 object instances in 19,994 images, following the standard RefCOCO [75] UNC partition scheme (train/val/testA/testB).

Appendix B Evaluation Metrics

For RIS, we use mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) as the evaluation metric. For GRES, we evaluate our model using three metrics: gIoU, cIoU, and N-acc on gRefCOCO [45]. The gIoU calculates the average IoU across all instances in an image, treating empty targets as true positives with an IoU of 1. The cIoU evaluates the ratio of intersection to union pixels. N-acc in gRefCOCO represents the proportion of correctly classified non-referent expressions.

Appendix C Additional Implementation Details

The model is trained using the Adam [33] optimizer with a learning rate of 1×10−41\times 10^{-4} and a batch size of 32. For the GRES task, the maximum sentence length is limited to 50 words, and the number of object queries is set to 20. The model is trained for 6 epochs, with the learning rate reduced by a factor of 0.1 at the 5th epoch. For the RIS task, the maximum sentence length is limited to 20 words, and the number of object queries is set to 10. The model is trained for 20 epochs, with the learning rate reduced by a factor of 0.1 at the 15th and 19th epoch. The experimental results are conducted in 8 NVIDIA A100(40G) GPUs. Ablation studies are conducted on the val set of gRefCOCO [45] without additional explanations.

For the large language model version, we employ LoRA [24] for efficient training, setting the rank to 8 and the alpha to 16. We train the model for 10 epochs on a mixed dataset comprising the RefCOCO series. The training batch size per GPU is set to 4, and we use a learning rate of 4e-5, with AdamW [52] as the optimizer.

Appendix D Additional Methodology

D.1 Text Similarity Metrics

Jaccard similarity is a set-based similarity measure that focuses on the presence of key terms, making it well-suited for comparing short texts. Given two text segments represented as word sets AA and BB, the Jaccard similarity is defined as:

J⁡(A,B)=|A∩B||A∪B|J(A,B)=\frac{|A\cap B|}{|A\cup B|} (9)

where A∩BA\cap B denotes the intersection of the word sets, and A∪BA\cup B represents their union.

Cosine similarity, on the other hand, is a vector-based measure that incorporates word frequency weights, making it more effective for longer texts. For vectorized text representations 𝐯1\mathbf{v}_{1} and 𝐯2\mathbf{v}_{2}, the cosine similarity is computed as:

cos⁡(θ)=𝐯1⋅𝐯2‖𝐯1‖​‖𝐯2‖\cos(\theta)=\frac{\mathbf{v}_{1}\cdot\mathbf{v}_{2}}{\|\mathbf{v}_{1}\|\|\mathbf{v}_{2}\|} (10)

where ⋅\cdot denotes the dot product, and ‖𝐯‖\|\mathbf{v}\| represents the Euclidean norm of the vector. To compute text similarity, we evaluate both set-based and vector-based similarities. The final similarity score is obtained by linearly combining the two measures:

Sfinal=12​(J⁡(A,B)+cos⁡(θ))S_{\text{final}}=\frac{1}{2}\left(J(A,B)+\cos(\theta)\right) (11)

Through experiments, we determine an optimal threshold TsT_{s}, above which two text segments are considered similar.

Appendix E Additional Experimental Results

E.1 Impact of the Number of Loopback Synergy Rounds

The multi-round interaction mechanism of loopback synergy, along with the auxiliary loss computation, introduces additional computational complexity during both forward and backward propagation. To evaluate the impact of different interaction rounds NrN_{r} on model performance and training efficiency, we conduct experiments. As shown in Fig. 7, we observe that increasing NrN_{r} leads to performance improvements, but at the cost of reduced training efficiency. Based on this trade-off, we select Nr=3N_{r}=3 as a compromise between performance and efficiency.

E.2 Impact of the Number of Object Queries

The effect of the number of object queries NqN_{q} on model performance is shown in Fig. 8. Given that the number of referents in the gRefCOCO [45] dataset typically does not exceed 10, we observe that increasing NqN_{q} leads to a decline in model performance. This performance degradation primarily arises because a larger number of object queries increases the probability of similar masks being assigned to each query, which in turn amplifies the ambiguity in the one-to-one matching process and makes the referent classification task more challenging. This additional complexity indirectly slows down convergence. Consequently, we select Nq=20N_{q}=20 as a balanced choice to optimize both performance and efficiency.

E.3 Impact of the Source of Non-referent Judgement

The non-referent is designed to determine whether the target referred to by the expression is present in the image, which directly impacts the model’s performance. we conduct experiments to investigate the influence of different sources of non-referent on performance. As shown in Table 9, the sources for non-referent judgment, denoted as query, image, and cls, correspond to the query from loopback synergy, the image features and the global features from the image-text pre-trained encoder, respectively. The results indicate that query significantly outperforms the other two alternatives in terms of non-referent discrimination performance. We attribute this superior performance to the fact that the cognition branch alone lacks the fine-grained spatial perception capabilities. In contrast, the query features, through multiple rounds of loopback synergy, progressively enhance the discrimination of non-referent.

E.4 Impact of the Weight Sharing in Loopback Synergy

The weights in the cognition decoder can either be shared or independent. we conducted experiments to compare the impact of weight-sharing and weight-independent of the cognition decoder on the performance. As shown in Table 10, the results demonstrate that the weight-independent strategy significantly outperforms the weight-sharing strategy in terms of performance. We attribute this to the fact that independent weights allow for a more precise representation of features at each round, mitigating the representation coupling issue caused by weight-sharing. This, in turn, facilitates more effective model training and optimization.

E.5 Loopback Efficiency Analysis

As shown in the Table 11, increasing the recurrence count from 1 to 3 leads to a 1.5% improvement in the cIoU metric, demonstrating the necessity of deeper interaction between the perception and understanding branches. However, further increasing the count to 5 yields only a marginal gain of 0.3% in cIoU, while significantly increasing both model parameters and training time. To balance performance and efficiency, we set the recurrence count to 3.

E.6 Performance on Video-Specific Datasets

As shown in Table 12, we report zero-shot performance on the Ref-YouTube-VOS [60] and MeVIS [16] datasets. Despite not utilizing temporal information, our DeRIS framework still achieves competitive results, demonstrating its strong potential for extension to video grounding scenarios.

Appendix F Qualitative Analyses

F.1 Comparison with Different Centric Architecture Models

Fig. 9 presents the visualization results of CRIS, LAVT, and DeRIS on the RefCOCOg test set. The results demonstrate that the DeRIS model effectively segments the referent targets in complex scenes, producing high-quality instance masks with clear boundaries and accurate segmentation. Moreover, the model successfully captures the fine-grained details of the referent targets. LAVT adopts a perception-centric architecture, exhibiting strong fine-grained perception capabilities. However, it struggles with comprehensive vision-language understanding. In contrast, CRIS (cognition-centric) excels in precise vision-language comprehension but lacks fine-grained perception, often resulting in coarse and imprecise contours. DeRIS integrates the strengths of both architectures, achieving a robust balance between fine-grained perception and semantic understanding.

F.2 Visualization of Instance Masks on gRefCOCO

Fig. 10 presents the visualization of instance masks with confidence scores greater than 0.5 on the gRefCOCO dataset. It can be observed that even in complex multi-object scenes, DeRIS accurately segments the target instances while ensuring strong textual relevance. This is attributed to its robust perceptual capabilities as a prerequisite, coupled with a powerful cognitive model for context understanding. Furthermore, even in challenging scenarios involving extremely small objects, such as the fourth sample, DeRIS remains capable of precisely capturing the target and assigning a high confidence score.

F.3 Visualization Analysis of the NSC Strategy

F.3.1 Non-Referent Target Scenarios

Fig. 11 illustrates the effectiveness of the NSC strategy in handling non-referent samples. Taking (a) as an example, the results demonstrate that without the NSC strategy, the model erroneously identifies the woman on the right, wearing a mixed-color dress, as the referent target with a confidence score of 1.00, leading to a clear misclassification. However, after applying the NSC strategy, the model correctly classifies this instance as a non-referent target, with its confidence score significantly reduced to 0.04, indicating a substantial improvement. This comparative experiment validates that the NSC strategy enhances the model’s ability to distinguish between visually similar distracting objects, thereby improving its robustness in recognizing non-referent instances within complex scenes.

F.3.2 Referent Existing Target Scenarios

Fig. 12 presents a performance comparison of the NSC strategy in scenarios involving referent targets. Taking (a) as an example, the results show that the ”velvet devil” pattern on the label of the second bottle and the floral pattern on the label of the third bottle are valid referent targets, while the other two bottles act as distracting instances. In the baseline model, without the NSC strategy, two common errors occur: false positives for the non-referent bottles (with confidence scores of 0.96 and 0.93), and a missed detection of the floral-patterned bottle, which has a confidence score of 0.64—below the detection threshold of 0.7.

After incorporating the NSC strategy during training, the model exhibits significant improvements: the confidence scores of the distracting samples decrease to 0.63 and 0.02, while the confidence score of the floral-patterned bottle rises to 0.96, successfully ensuring accurate detection. These results indicate that the NSC strategy enhances the model’s ability to suppress false positives in complex scenes by establishing more differentiated representations between targets while significantly improving its detection capability for weakly salient referent targets.

F.4 Visualization of Different Textual Conditions on gRefCOCO

Fig. 13 presents the segmentation results under different textual conditions on the gRefCOCO dataset. Through visualizing the model’s response to various textual expressions for the same image, we observe that DeRIS demonstrates strong capabilities in comprehending both text and images, as well as effectively identifying cases where the referent object is absent. Even in scenarios involving long and complex textual descriptions, visually intricate targets, and challenging cases with no referent object, the model exhibits remarkable robustness and discrimination ability.

F.5 Visualization of RefCOCO/+/g Dataset

Fig. 14 presents the visualization results on the RefCOCO/+/g dataset. In one-to-one correspondence scenarios, DeRIS also demonstrates strong performance without requiring additional architectural modifications. The model seamlessly adapts to single-object, multi-object, and absent-object scenarios, maintaining robust and consistent performance across diverse cases.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.
